title: Generalized Stage III Grade C Periodontitis in Poorly Controlled Diabetes
short: 54M • ASA III • T2DM HbA1c 8.4% • 15 cig/day

patient.medical_history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus × 12 years (most recent HbA1c 8.4%); hypertension; BMI 31. No prior periodontal surgery.
patient.medications: Metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly.
patient.social_history: Smokes 15 cigarettes/day × 25 years (18.8 pack-years). Occasional alcohol. Infrequent dental care.
patient.chief_complaint: My gums bleed when I brush and my front teeth are drifting. I was told I need implants for the back teeth.

clinical_findings.extraoral: No lymphadenopathy. TMJ exam within normal limits.
clinical_findings.intraoral: Fair oral hygiene. Generalized marginal erythema. Pathologic migration of #8 and #9 with a 2 mm diastema. Missing #3, #14, #19.
clinical_findings.periodontal: Generalized probing depths 5–8 mm; CAL 5–7 mm. BOP 62%. Furcation Glickman II on #18 and #30. Mobility I–II on #8, #9, #24, #25. No active suppuration today. Full-mouth plaque score 48%.
clinical_findings.radiographs: FMX: generalized horizontal bone loss to the middle third of roots (≈40–50%). Angular defects #18 distal and #30 mesial. No obvious pulpal caries. Moderate pneumatization of the maxillary sinuses.

flags: HbA1c ≥7.0% → Grade C diabetes modifier
≥10 cigarettes/day → Grade C smoking modifier
CAL ≥5 mm + mid-third bone loss + furcation II = Stage III
Active periodontitis + hyperglycemia = implant risk
guidelines: 2018 AAP/EFP World Workshop Classification of Periodontal and Peri-Implant Diseases
ITI Consensus (implants in patients with periodontitis and diabetes)

vignette.demographics: 54-year-old male, ASA III. T2DM (HbA1c 8.4%), hypertension, BMI 31. Smokes 15 cig/day × 25 years. Metformin, lisinopril, atorvastatin. NKDA.
vignette.chief: Gum bleeding with brushing and drifting of the upper front teeth. Interested in posterior implants.
vignette.clinical: Generalized erythema. Pathologic migration #8–9. Missing #3, #14, #19. PD 5–8 mm, CAL 5–7 mm, BOP 62%. Furcation II #18 and #30. Mobility I–II anteriorly. Plaque 48%.
vignette.endo: No lingering thermal pain. Percussion negative except mild tenderness #18. Sensibility testing WNL on remaining teeth.
vignette.radio: Generalized mid-third bone loss; angular defects #18-D and #30-M. Sinus pneumatization. No periapical rarefactions of endodontic origin.

questions.q: Using the 2018 AAP/EFP classification, the most accurate periodontal diagnosis is:
options: Generalized Stage II Grade B periodontitis
Generalized Stage III Grade C periodontitis
Generalized Stage IV Grade C periodontitis
Molar-incisor pattern Stage III Grade C periodontitis (formerly ‘aggressive’)
questions.explanation: Stage III is defined by interdental CAL ≥5 mm, radiographic bone loss extending to the middle third of the root, and tooth loss due to periodontitis of ≤4 teeth, plus complexity factors (intrabony defects, furcation II/III). Stage IV requires ≥5 teeth lost to periodontitis and/or loss of masticatory function requiring complex rehabilitation (bite collapse, severe drift, fewer than 10 opposing pairs). Here function is largely intact and only three teeth are missing, so Stage III—not IV—is correct. Grade C is assigned because of two grade modifiers: smoking ≥10 cigarettes/day AND diabetes with HbA1c ≥7.0%. Stage II is too mild (typically coronal-third bone loss and CAL 3–4 mm). The 1999 ‘aggressive periodontitis’ terminology and a molar-incisor pattern are not supported by this generalized adult presentation.

questions.q: The patient wants posterior implants placed as soon as possible. The most evidence-based next step is:
options: Place implants immediately; a history of periodontitis does not affect implant survival once the teeth are gone
Extract remaining ‘hopeless’ teeth and immediately load a full-arch prosthesis
Initiate cause-related periodontal therapy, smoking-cessation support, and medical optimization of glycemic control before any elective implant placement
Prescribe a 21-day course of amoxicillin–metronidazole and schedule implant surgery in 2 weeks
questions.explanation: Active periodontitis and poorly controlled diabetes (HbA1c commonly cited threshold ≥8% for elective implant surgery) are associated with higher rates of implant failure and peri-implantitis. The 2018 World Workshop and ITI consensus recommend completing cause-related periodontal therapy and modifying risk factors (smoking, hyperglycemia) before elective implant therapy. Antibiotics alone do not replace mechanical debridement and risk-factor control. Immediate full-arch conversion in untreated Stage III Grade C disease is not first-line. Residual periodontal pathogens and uncontrolled hyperglycemia should be addressed first.

title: Peri-implantitis at an Esthetic-Zone Implant — 2018 Case Definition
short: 47F • ASA II • Implant #9 × 6 years • Cement-retained crown

patient.medical_history: Well-controlled hypothyroidism. Former smoker (quit 8 years ago). No diabetes.
patient.social_history: Former smoker, 10 pack-years, quit 2018. Drinks 3–4 glasses of wine/week.
patient.chief_complaint: The gum around my front implant looks red and has started to bleed, and I think the tooth looks longer.

clinical_findings.extraoral: High smile line; 3 mm of implant restoration visible on full smile. No swelling of the lip.
clinical_findings.intraoral: Bone-level implant #9 with cement-retained lithium-disilicate crown. Mid-facial recession 2 mm compared with #8. Peri-implant mucosa erythematous. Cement-like deposits suspected at the mesial margin on transillumination.
clinical_findings.periodontal: Implant #9: PD 6 mm mid-facial, 7 mm mesial, 5 mm distal; BOP+; light suppuration on probing mesially. Natural teeth: PD ≤3 mm, BOP 8%. Keratinized mucosa on the facial of #9 is 1 mm, thin phenotype.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Periapical + CBCT: crestal bone 3.5 mm apical to the implant platform mesially (baseline radiograph 5 years ago showed <1 mm remodeling). Saucer-shaped defect, no mobility of the implant. No adjacent periapical pathosis.
clinical_findings.other: No previous probing chart for the implant is available from the restoring dentist.

flags: PD ≥6 mm + BOP + suppuration + ≥3 mm bone loss from baseline = peri-implantitis
Cement-retained esthetic-zone crown — residual cement risk
Thin phenotype + high smile line = esthetic stakes
Penicillin allergy
guidelines: 2017/2018 World Workshop peri-implant health, mucositis, and peri-implantitis case definitions
ITI Treatment Guide — managing peri-implantitis

vignette.demographics: 47-year-old female, ASA II. Hypothyroidism on levothyroxine. Former smoker, quit 8 years. Penicillin allergy (rash).
vignette.chief: Red, bleeding gum around the front implant; restoration looks longer.
vignette.clinical: Cement-retained implant crown #9. Facial recession 2 mm. PD 5–7 mm with BOP and mesial suppuration. Thin phenotype, 1 mm keratinized mucosa. Natural dentition periodontally stable.
vignette.radio: 3.5 mm mesial bone loss from platform versus <1 mm on a 5-year-old baseline PA. Saucerized defect. Implant not mobile.

questions.q: According to the 2018 World Workshop, the peri-implant diagnosis at #9 is:
options: Peri-implant health with remodeling
Peri-implant mucositis
Peri-implantitis
Hard- and soft-tissue deficiency without inflammation
questions.explanation: Peri-implantitis requires inflammation (BOP and/or suppuration) PLUS progressive bone loss. When baseline radiographs exist, any bone loss beyond initial remodeling plus BOP is diagnostic; in the absence of baseline data, the workshop threshold is PD ≥6 mm with BOP and bone levels ≥3 mm apical to the intraosseous portion of the implant. This case meets both: documented progression from <1 mm to 3.5 mm AND PD 6–7 mm with BOP/suppuration. Mucositis is inflammation without bone loss beyond remodeling. Soft-tissue deficiency alone does not capture the progressive osseous defect and suppuration.

questions.q: After nonsurgical debridement and cement removal, the most appropriate next surgical consideration for this esthetic-zone defect is:
options: Apically positioned flap with implantoplasty as first-line, accepting further recession
Reconstructive (regenerative) approach for the contained saucerized defect, with counseling that complete papilla/facial-contour recovery is unpredictable
Immediate explantation and chairside conversion to a cantilever pontic from #8
Systemic clindamycin for 10 days as definitive therapy because of the penicillin allergy
questions.explanation: Contained, saucerized peri-implantitis defects are the phenotype most likely to benefit from reconstructive therapy (e.g., access + decontamination + graft/membrane) after infection control. In the esthetic zone, resective therapy/implantoplasty predictably increases recession and is poorly suited to a high smile line. Explantation is reserved for mobility, unresectable/non-reconstructable advanced loss, or failed reconstructive attempts—not as the automatic first surgical step. Antibiotics are adjunctive at most; clindamycin is not definitive therapy and is avoided when possible because of C. difficile risk. Informed consent must emphasize that pink-esthetic recovery is uncertain.

title: Stage IV Periodontitis with Bite Collapse — Sequencing Full-Mouth Rehabilitation
short: 62F • ASA II • Pathologic migration • Posterior bite collapse

patient.medical_history: Osteopenia (not on antiresorptives). Controlled hypertension.
patient.medications: Amlodipine 5 mg daily; calcium + vitamin D.
patient.social_history: Never smoker. Retired teacher.
patient.chief_complaint: My teeth have shifted, I can’t chew on my back teeth, and my bite feels collapsed. I want a fixed smile.

clinical_findings.extraoral: Reduced lower facial third. Overclosed appearance at rest.
clinical_findings.intraoral: Splayed maxillary incisors with diastemas. Flared #7–10. Missing #2, #3, #14, #15, #18, #19, #30, #31 (history consistent with periodontal loss). Super-erupted #4 and #13. Occlusal plane discrepancy. Remaining molars #1 and #16 non-functional.
clinical_findings.periodontal: CAL 6–9 mm on remaining dentition. PD 4–7 mm after a recent SRP series (BOP now 28%, was 70%). Mobility II–III on #7–10, #23–26. Fewer than 10 occluding pairs. Fremitus on all maxillary incisors.
clinical_findings.occlusion: Loss of posterior support. Traumatic occlusion on flared anteriors. Reduced OVD clinically. No TMD pain.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Generalized bone loss to apical third on remaining anterior teeth. Ridge atrophy in posterior sextants. #23–26 with <30% remaining bone.

flags: ≥5 teeth lost to periodontitis + masticatory dysfunction = Stage IV
Bite collapse / pathologic migration
Need for complex rehabilitation (prosthetic-periodontal sequencing)
Anterior teeth with hopeless/questionable prognosis
guidelines: 2018 AAP/EFP staging — Stage IV complexity (masticatory dysfunction, bite collapse, <20 remaining teeth / <10 opposing pairs)
ITI / prosthodontic sequencing: control disease → provisionalize → reconstruct

vignette.demographics: 62-year-old female, ASA II. Osteopenia (no antiresorptives). HTN on amlodipine. Never smoker.
vignette.chief: Shifting teeth, inability to chew posteriorly, collapsed bite; desires a fixed smile.
vignette.clinical: Splayed maxillary incisors, diastemas, missing multiple posteriors to periodontal disease, super-eruption, fremitus, mobility II–III anteriors. <10 occluding pairs. Reduced OVD appearance.
vignette.endo: Anteriors respond to cold without lingering. No draining sinuses.
vignette.radio: Apical-third bone loss remaining anteriors. Posterior ridge atrophy. Hopeless bone support #23–26.

questions.q: This patient’s periodontitis is best staged as Stage IV primarily because of:
options: Probing depths of 6–7 mm alone
BOP of 28% after SRP
Tooth loss due to periodontitis of ≥5 teeth plus masticatory dysfunction / bite collapse requiring complex rehabilitation
Osteopenia, which automatically upstages any periodontitis
questions.explanation: Stage IV is distinguished from Stage III by complexity and function: ≥5 teeth lost to periodontitis, plus bite collapse, pathologic migration, less than 10 opposing pairs, and the need for complex rehabilitation to restore function. Deep pockets alone can occur in Stage III. Post-SRP BOP of 28% describes current inflammatory control, not stage. Osteopenia is not a staging criterion (smoking and diabetes are grade modifiers, not staging rules).

questions.q: The most defensible initial rehabilitation sequence is:
options: Immediate full-arch extraction and same-day loaded FP1 prostheses in both arches

Stabilize remaining strategic teeth, extract hopeless teeth, use provisional restorations to re-establish OVD/plane, then definitive implant-supported rehabilitation after soft- and hard-tissue management
Splint the mobile anteriors with composite and observe 24 months before any extraction
Maxillary complete denture against a mandibular Kennedy Class I RPD as the only evidence-based option
questions.explanation: Stage IV care is a periodontal–prosthodontic project: control inflammation, remove hopeless teeth, provisionally restore OVD and the occlusal plane, then reconstruct (often implant-supported) after appropriate grafting/soft-tissue management. Immediate full-arch conversion can be appropriate in selected arches after planning, but ‘same-day FP1 both arches’ without disease control, ridge assessment, and smile-line analysis is not automatically correct—especially with apical-third bone loss and atrophic posteriors that may preclude FP1. Composite splinting of hopeless mandibular incisors delays the inevitable without restoring posterior support. A CD/RPD is a valid alternative if implants are declined, but it is not the only evidence-based path when the patient desires a fixed solution and is a surgical candidate.

title: RT2 Recession, Thin Phenotype, and Root-Coverage Strategy
short: 29F • ASA I • Cairo RT2 #24–25 • Orthodontic history

patient.medical_history: Noncontributory. Completed orthodontics at age 16 (four premolar extractions).
patient.social_history: Never smoker. Competitive runner. Aggressive toothbrushing history (hard brush, horizontal technique).
patient.chief_complaint: The gums on my lower front teeth have receded and the teeth look long. I’m getting sensitivity to cold.

clinical_findings.extraoral: Medium smile line. Mandibular incisors visible at rest.
clinical_findings.intraoral: Thin periodontal phenotype. Recession on #24 (4 mm) and #25 (3.5 mm) with interdental papilla loss of ≈1 mm. Scalloped, thin gingiva. Abrasion notches at CEJ. Residual orthodontic mandibular incisor proclination.
clinical_findings.periodontal: Cairo Recession Type 2 (RT2) #24–25: gingival margin apical to CEJ with interproximal attachment loss less than the buccal CAL. PD 2–3 mm, BOP 6%. KT 1 mm facial of #24–25. No mobility. Maxillary canines have 1–2 mm RT1 recession.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Bitewings/PAs: interproximal bone slightly apical to the CEJ at #24–25 (≈1 mm), consistent with RT2. No calculus on radiographs. Roots are not short.

flags: Cairo RT2 (not Miller still, but RT2 ≈ Miller III-ish interdental loss)
Thin phenotype + 1 mm KT
Traumatic hygiene + residual proclination
Complete root coverage less predictable than RT1
guidelines: Cairo recession types (RT1–RT3) — 2011; adopted in 2018 Workshop mucogingival conditions
AAP Regeneration Workshop — root coverage (CAF + CTG gold standard in RT1; reduced predictability in RT2)

vignette.demographics: 29-year-old healthy female, ASA I. Prior orthodontics with premolar extractions. OCP. Never smoker.
vignette.chief: Lower-incisor recession, long-looking teeth, cold sensitivity.
vignette.clinical: Thin phenotype. Recession 4 mm #24 and 3.5 mm #25 with mild papilla loss. KT 1 mm. Abrasion notches. PD 2–3 mm, low BOP. Residual incisor proclination.
vignette.endo: Normal cold response without lingering; sensitivity is hydrodynamic from exposed dentin.
vignette.radio: Mild interproximal bone loss at #24–25 consistent with RT2. No periapical pathosis.

questions.q: The recession on #24–25 is best classified as:
options: Cairo RT1 (no interproximal attachment loss) — complete coverage highly predictable
Cairo RT2 (interproximal attachment loss ≤ buccal CAL) — complete coverage possible but less predictable
Cairo RT3 (interproximal loss greater than buccal) — root coverage not expected
Stillman’s cleft from occlusal trauma, which is not a recession type
questions.explanation: Cairo RT2 is recession with interproximal attachment loss that is less than or equal to the buccal CAL—matching the mild papilla/bone loss here. RT1 has no interproximal loss and the highest complete-coverage rates. RT3 has interproximal loss greater than buccal CAL; complete coverage is not an expected outcome. Stillman’s cleft is a morphologic descriptor, not a substitute for Cairo typing. The 2018 Workshop endorsed Cairo types for mucogingival deformities.

questions.q: The most evidence-based surgical plan to maximize root coverage and phenotype modification is:
options: Coronally advanced flap alone (no graft)
Free gingival graft as a first-line root-coverage procedure for esthetic mandibular incisors
Coronally advanced flap or tunnel technique combined with a connective-tissue graft (or substitute in selected cases), plus hygiene re-instruction and consideration of minor orthodontic repositioning
Elective extraction of #24–25 and immediately placed narrow-diameter implants
questions.explanation: CAF (or tunnel) + CTG remains the gold-standard combination for root coverage and for increasing gingival thickness/KT in a thin phenotype. CAF alone underperforms in thin phenotype and RT2. Free gingival grafts reliably increase KT but yield inferior color match and less root coverage in the esthetic zone. Extraction/implants for RT2 recession in vital, restorable mandibular incisors is not indicated. Adjunctive control of traumatic hygiene and residual proclination improves long-term stability.

title: Peri-implant Mucositis vs Early Peri-implantitis at a Posterior Implant
short: 51M • ASA II • Implant #30 × 18 months • No baseline radiograph

patient.medical_history: Well-controlled T2DM, HbA1c 6.6%. Overweight.
patient.social_history: Never smoker. Missed two implant-maintenance visits in the past year.
patient.chief_complaint: The hygienist said the gum around my implant is bleeding. It doesn’t hurt.

clinical_findings.intraoral: Bone-level implant #30 with screw-retained zirconia crown. Emergence slightly over-contoured. Food entrapment reported.
clinical_findings.periodontal: Implant #30: PD 5 mm all surfaces, BOP+ at 3 of 4 sites, no suppuration, no recession, implant not mobile. Natural teeth: history of Stage II Grade A periodontitis, now PD ≤4 mm, BOP 12% in SPT.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Current PA: bone level 2.0 mm apical to the implant platform. No prior implant radiograph can be located. No thread exposure on the radiograph. Adjacent #29, #31 WNL.

flags: No baseline implant radiograph — use 2018 absence-of-data criteria
PD 5 mm + BOP without ≥3 mm bone loss threshold
Over-contour / hygiene access
History of periodontitis = lifelong peri-implant risk
guidelines: 2018 World Workshop: if no previous exam, peri-implantitis = BOP/suppuration + PD ≥6 mm + bone level ≥3 mm apical to intraosseous portion
SPT / peri-implant maintenance intervals (3–6 months in high-risk patients)

vignette.demographics: 51-year-old male, ASA II. T2DM HbA1c 6.6% on metformin. Never smoker. History of Stage II periodontitis in SPT. Missed two maintenance visits.
vignette.chief: Asymptomatic bleeding around implant #30 noted at hygiene visit.
vignette.clinical: Screw-retained #30 implant crown, slightly over-contoured. PD 5 mm, BOP, no pus, no mobility.
vignette.radio: Bone 2.0 mm from platform. No baseline film available. No radiographic thread exposure.

questions.q: In the absence of a baseline radiograph, the 2018 case definition that best fits implant #30 is:
options: Peri-implant health
Peri-implant mucositis
Peri-implantitis
Failing implant (osseointegration never achieved)
questions.explanation: Without a previous examination, peri-implantitis is defined as BOP/suppuration, PD ≥6 mm, AND bone levels ≥3 mm apical to the intraosseous portion of the implant. This implant has BOP and PD 5 mm with only 2 mm of radiographic bone from the platform—below both numeric thresholds—so the diagnosis is peri-implant mucositis (inflammation without the bone-loss criteria). Health requires no BOP. A ‘failing’ implant implies mobility/lack of osseointegration, which is absent. Treat mucositis aggressively; it is reversible and is the precursor to peri-implantitis.

questions.q: The most appropriate management at this visit is:
options: Surgical regenerative therapy of the ‘intrabony implant defect’
Explantation because of the history of periodontitis
Nonsurgical peri-implant debridement, contour/hygiene-access modification as needed, reinforced home care, and a shortened maintenance interval (typically 3 months)
Empiric 7-day amoxicillin–metronidazole without mechanical debridement
questions.explanation: Peri-implant mucositis is managed by mechanical biofilm disruption, improving cleansability (recontour over-contoured restorations), and maintenance—analogous to gingivitis therapy. Surgery is not first-line without peri-implantitis-level bone loss. History of periodontitis raises risk and justifies tighter SPT, not automatic explantation of a stable implant. Systemic antibiotics without debridement are not indicated for mucositis.

title: Cracked Mandibular Molar vs Vertical Root Fracture
short: 48M • ASA I • #30 biting pain • Large MOD amalgam

patient.medical_history: Noncontributory.
patient.social_history: Never smoker. Clenches during work stress.
patient.chief_complaint: Sharp pain when I bite on my lower right molar, especially on release. It started 3 weeks ago.

clinical_findings.intraoral: #30 with a large MOD amalgam, no cusp coverage. No sinus tract. Adjacent restorations conservative.
clinical_findings.periodontal: PD 2–3 mm around #30 except a narrow isolated 6 mm probing defect on the mid-distal surface. No generalized periodontitis.
clinical_findings.endodontic_testing: Cold: lingering 12 seconds #30 (adjacent teeth <3 s). EPT: 38 (#29=18, #31=20). Percussion: mild. Palpation: negative. Bite test (Tooth Slooth): sharp pain on release on the distolingual cusp.
clinical_findings.radiographs: PA/bitewing: deep restoration close to pulp horns; no obvious PA rarefaction; no J-shaped lesion. Cracks not visible radiographically. CBCT (limited FOV): no vertical bone loss along a root surface; slight PDL widening at the distal root.

flags: Pain on release = classic cracked-tooth symptom
Lingering cold + elevated EPT = symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Isolated narrow deep probing raises VRF concern but is not pathognomonic
No J-shaped lesion / no CBCT vertical defect
guidelines: AAE Colleagues for Excellence — Cracking the Cracked Tooth Code; AAE Diagnostic Terminology
AAE/AAOMR CBCT position statement (limited FOV for inconclusive intraoral imaging)

vignette.demographics: 48-year-old healthy male, ASA I. Clenching history. NKDA.
vignette.chief: Sharp biting pain on lower right molar, worse on release, 3 weeks.
vignette.clinical: Large uncrowned MOD amalgam #30. Isolated narrow 6 mm mid-distal probing. Rest of periodontium WNL.
vignette.endo: Lingering cold 12 s; EPT 38 vs 18–20 neighbors; mild percussion; pain on release distolingual cusp.
vignette.radio: Deep restoration, no PA radiolucency, no J-shaped lesion. Limited-FOV CBCT: no VRF-type vertical defect; mild distal PDL widening.

questions.q: The AAE pulpal and apical diagnoses for #30 are:
options: Reversible pulpitis; normal apical tissues
Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis; symptomatic apical periodontitis
Pulp necrosis; chronic apical abscess
Previously treated; asymptomatic apical periodontitis
questions.explanation: Lingering thermal pain (> a few seconds) and an elevated EPT indicate symptomatic irreversible pulpitis, not reversible pulpitis (momentary pain that does not linger). Mild percussion tenderness establishes symptomatic apical periodontitis even without a radiographic rarefaction. There is no sinus tract (so not a chronic apical abscess) and the pulp is not necrotic (still responds to cold/EPT). The tooth has not been previously treated.

questions.q: The isolated 6 mm probing depth most correctly influences the plan how?
options: It proves a complete vertical root fracture; extract immediately
It is expected with all cracked teeth and can be ignored

It raises suspicion for a crack extending onto the root; after RCT and a full-coverage restoration, re-evaluate the isolated defect—extraction is indicated if a true VRF with a J-shaped lesion/hopeless periodontium is confirmed
It requires immediate root amputation of the distal root
questions.explanation: An isolated narrow deep pocket can be associated with a crack that has reached the root or with VRF, but it is not pathognomonic—especially without a J-shaped lesion, mobility, or CBCT vertical bone loss. For a cracked tooth with a vital/irreversibly inflamed pulp, standard care is RCT plus cuspal coverage; many isolated defects stabilize after occlusion is controlled and the crack is ‘crowned over.’ Proven VRF in a molar (J-shaped lesion, split, hopeless isolated defect after exploration) is generally an extraction indication, not root amputation as first-line in a non-strategic distal root with an intact mesial root still unrestored. Immediate extraction without a diagnosis of VRF overtreats a potentially savable cracked tooth.

title: Avulsed Mature Maxillary Central Incisor — Extraoral Dry Time 70 Minutes
short: 16M • ASA I • Avulsion #8 • Dry time 70 min • School athletic field

patient.medical_history: Healthy. Up-to-date tetanus (Tdap 3 years ago). No allergies.
patient.social_history: High-school soccer. No mouthguard at the time of injury.
patient.chief_complaint: Coach brought the tooth in a paper towel. It was knocked out about 70 minutes ago. He wants it put back.

clinical_findings.extraoral: No loss of consciousness. GCS 15. Lip laceration already sutured at urgent care. No midface mobility.
clinical_findings.intraoral: Socket #8 filled with clot. #7 and #9 intact, not mobile. No alveolar fracture palpable. Occlusion unchanged. Tooth #8: closed apex, debris on root, PDL remnants dried, no gross root fracture on inspection.
clinical_findings.endodontic_testing: #7 and #9: normal cold and percussion at presentation (will require serial follow-up).
clinical_findings.radiographs: PA of the socket: no root fragments, no alveolar fracture obvious. PA of the avulsed tooth extraorally: closed apex, no root fracture.

flags: Closed apex + extraoral dry time >60 min → PDL non-viable (IADT 2020)
Ankylosis / replacement resorption expected
Flexible splint 2 weeks still indicated if reimplanted
RCT timing: extraoral RCT or within 7–10 days
guidelines: IADT 2020 Guidelines for the Management of Traumatic Dental Injuries — Avulsion of Permanent Teeth
AAE recommended guidelines for treatment of traumatic dental injuries

vignette.demographics: 16-year-old healthy male, ASA I. Tdap 3 years ago. Soccer injury, no mouthguard. No LOC.
vignette.chief: Avulsed #8, stored dry in paper towel, extraoral time 70 minutes. Patient and parent request replantation.
vignette.clinical: Closed-apex #8 with dried PDL. Socket with clot, no alveolar fracture. Adjacent teeth intact.
vignette.endo: Adjacent teeth currently responsive. Avulsed tooth not tested (out of mouth).
vignette.radio: Empty socket without retained fragments. Extraoral PA: closed apex, no root fracture.

questions.q: According to IADT 2020, the biologically correct statement about this closed-apex avulsion with 70 minutes dry time is:
options: The PDL is likely still viable; immediate replantation has an excellent long-term prognosis
The PDL is non-viable; replantation may still be performed after removing necrotic PDL, with the expected long-term outcome of ankylosis/replacement resorption
Replantation is contraindicated once dry time exceeds 20 minutes
The tooth must be discarded; only an immediate implant is acceptable in a 16-year-old
questions.explanation: IADT 2020 treats extraoral dry time >60 minutes as non-viable PDL. Replantation is still often recommended (especially in a growing 16-year-old) to preserve the alveolar ridge and delay a prosthetic decision, but the expected biologic outcome is ankylosis and replacement resorption. Prognosis is not ‘excellent.’ The 20-minute figure is outdated as an absolute contraindication. Immediate implant placement in a 16-year-old with incomplete facial growth is generally deferred because of infraocclusion risk; ridge preservation via replantation or a temporary prosthetic is preferred.

questions.q: If the tooth is replanted, the IADT-congruent endodontic and splinting protocol is:
options: Rigid stainless-steel wire splint for 4 months; delay RCT until a PA lesion appears
Flexible splint for 2 weeks; initiate RCT extraorally or within 7–10 days (corticosteroid/antibiotic or Ca(OH)2 medicament); consider doxycycline (age >12) and tetanus status
No splint; regenerative endodontics because the patient is under 18
Extraoral RCT, rigid splint 8 weeks, and mandatory systemic clindamycin
questions.explanation: For avulsion of a closed-apex tooth, IADT recommends a flexible splint for 2 weeks (not a long rigid splint, which promotes ankylosis). Because the PDL is non-viable and the apex is closed, pulp revascularization will not occur—RCT should be started extraorally before replantation or within 7–10 days, with an intracanal medicament. Systemic antibiotics are suggested (doxycycline preferred >12 years as an anti-resorptive adjunct; amoxicillin is an alternative); tetanus is updated if needed. Regenerative protocols are for immature necrotic teeth, not mature avulsed teeth. Clindamycin is not the IADT first-line antibiotic.

title: External Cervical Resorption (Patel 3D) of a Maxillary Central
short: 35F • ASA I • Pink spot #9 • History of orthodontics + trauma

patient.medical_history: Noncontributory. Orthodontics as a teen. Childhood concussion of #9 (no RCT).
patient.social_history: Never smoker.
patient.chief_complaint: A pink spot showed up near the gum of my front tooth. It doesn’t hurt.

clinical_findings.intraoral: Pink discoloration in the cervical third of #9 on the mesial-facial. Probe catches a subgingival defect. No sinus tract. Gingiva otherwise healthy.
clinical_findings.periodontal: PD 3 mm except 5 mm at the mesial-facial defect of #9, bleeding from the resorption cavity. No mobility.
clinical_findings.endodontic_testing: Cold: normal, non-lingering #9 (same as #8). EPT: 22 (#8=20). Percussion/palpation negative.
clinical_findings.radiographs: PA: irregular cervical radiolucency superimposed on the root canal outline, with the canal space still traceable (pathognomonic for external rather than internal resorption). Limited-FOV CBCT (Patel): portal of entry at the CEJ mesial-facial, lesion confined to cervical third, perilesional resorption extending <90° of the circumference, pulp not perforated (Patel height 1, circumferential 1, height/pulp P—i.e., 1-1-P).

flags: Pink spot + vital pulp = classic ECR, not internal resorption
Canal outline visible through the lesion on PA = external process
CBCT mandatory for Patel 3D classification and restorability
History of ortho + trauma = ECR risk factors
guidelines: European Society of Endodontology position statement on ECR; Patel 3D classification (2018)
AAE/AAOMR CBCT position statement

vignette.demographics: 35-year-old healthy female. Childhood trauma to #9; prior orthodontics. ASA I.
vignette.chief: Asymptomatic pink spot at the cervical of #9.
vignette.clinical: Cervical pink spot mesial-facial #9; subgingival catch; PD 5 mm at the defect only. Tooth not mobile.
vignette.endo: Vital pulp — normal cold and EPT compared with #8. No percussion tenderness.
vignette.radio: PA: cervical irregular lucency with canal outline still visible. CBCT: cervical-third ECR, <90° circumference, pulp not perforated (Patel 1-1-P).

questions.q: The resorptive process is best diagnosed as:
options: Internal inflammatory resorption requiring immediate RCT
External cervical resorption with a vital pulp
External inflammatory (infection-related) resorption from pulp necrosis
Replacement resorption (ankylosis) after trauma
questions.explanation: ECR (invasive cervical resorption) originates at the cervical PDL/CEJ, often presents as a pink spot, and commonly occurs with a vital pulp. Internal resorption starts within the pulp canal (which would appear ballooned, with the canal outline lost). External inflammatory resorption is driven by a necrotic infected pulp and typically occurs more apically/laterally on the root, not as a cervical pink spot with a vital response. Replacement resorption is ankylosis (metallic percussion, infraocclusion), not a pink cervical lesion. Vitality testing plus the PA finding of a preserved canal outline distinguishes ECR from internal resorption; CBCT confirms.

questions.q: For Patel 1-1-P (cervical, limited circumference, pulp intact), the most appropriate first-line treatment is:
options: Extraction and immediate implant because ECR always progresses to the pulp
External surgical repair (flap, complete removal of resorptive tissue, restoration) with pulp preservation if possible; RCT only if the pulp is entered or subsequently inflamed
Internal bleaching only
Observation indefinitely because the pulp is vital
questions.explanation: Localized cervical ECR with limited circumferential spread and an intact pulp is managed by complete excavation of the resorptive tissue (often via a flap) and restoration (GI/composite/bioceramic), aiming to keep the tooth and, when feasible, the pulp. RCT is added if the pulp is perforated or becomes irreversible. Extraction is reserved for advanced Patel classes (supracrestal/circumferential/apical extent that leaves the tooth unrestorable). Internal bleaching treats discoloration from blood-breakdown products in necrotic/treated teeth, not ECR. Observation of an accessible, progressive resorptive defect is not appropriate—ECR is aggressive even when the pulp is still vital.

title: Persistent Apical Periodontitis on #14 — Missed MB2
short: 41M • ASA I • RCT #14 two years ago • Intermittent sinus tract

patient.medical_history: Noncontributory.
patient.social_history: Never smoker.
patient.chief_complaint: A pimple on the gum above my upper left molar comes and goes. The tooth was root-canaled two years ago and crowned.

clinical_findings.intraoral: PFM crown #14 with adequate apparent margins. Palatal sinus tract traces with gutta-percha toward the MB root. No deep probing (PD ≤3 mm). No mobility. No occlusal prematurity.
clinical_findings.endodontic_testing: Percussion mildly tender. Palpation tender over the MB vestibule. Tooth does not respond to cold (previously treated).
clinical_findings.radiographs: PA: short fill of a single MB canal; untreated second MB canal suspected. PA rarefaction 5 mm at MB root apex. Limited-FOV CBCT: missed MB2 joining the MB1 in the apical third (Weine II / Vertucci II), periapical hypodensity on MB root, palatal and DB fills adequate, no VRF signs, sinus floor not perforated.

flags: Chronic apical abscess (sinus tract) on a previously treated tooth
Missed MB2 — most common cause of maxillary molar failure
CBCT: no VRF, restorable tooth → NSRCT first-line
Surgery reserved if retreatment not feasible or fails
guidelines: AAE Diagnostic Terminology (previously treated; chronic apical abscess)
AAE/AAOMR CBCT; ESE quality guidelines — orthograde retreatment preferred when the cause is technical and the tooth is restorable

vignette.demographics: 41-year-old healthy male. RCT and crown #14 two years ago.
vignette.chief: Intermittent palatal gum boil above the upper left molar.
vignette.clinical: Crown #14. Palatal sinus tract traces to MB root. PD ≤3 mm, no mobility.
vignette.endo: Previously treated. Mild percussion and MB palpation tenderness. No cold response.
vignette.radio: Short single MB fill; 5 mm MB PA lesion. CBCT: missed MB2 (Vertucci II), no VRF, other canals adequate.

questions.q: The AAE diagnoses for #14 are:
options: Previously initiated therapy; acute apical abscess
Previously treated; chronic apical abscess
Previously treated; symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Normal pulp; chronic apical abscess
questions.explanation: The tooth has existing RCT, so the pulpal diagnosis is ‘previously treated,’ not previously initiated and not a normal/irreversible pulp (those apply to untreated pulps). A sinus tract defines a chronic apical abscess (suppurative apical periodontitis), not an acute apical abscess (rapid swelling, no chronic tract). Irreversible pulpitis cannot be diagnosed on a previously treated tooth.

questions.q: The most appropriate first-line treatment is:
options: Immediate apicoectomy of the MB root without addressing MB2
Extraction and implant because persistent lesions after RCT never heal
Orthograde nonsurgical retreatment through the crown (or after crown removal) to locate and disinfect MB2, then restore with a well-sealed core/crown
Long-term antibiotics until the sinus tract closes
questions.explanation: When failure is due to a missed canal and the tooth is periodontally sound without VRF, orthograde retreatment is first-line and has high healing potential. Apical surgery without treating MB2 leaves the source of infection. Persistent lesions often heal after the missed anatomy is addressed; extraction is not mandated. Antibiotics do not sterilize an untreated canal system and are not a therapy for chronic apical abscess. Surgery is considered if retreatment is not feasible (posts/irretrievable obstructions) or if a lesion persists after adequate orthograde disinfection.

title: Immature Necrotic Central Incisor — Regenerative Endodontics vs Apexification
short: 10F • ASA I • #8 necrotic • Open apex • History of intrusion

patient.medical_history: Healthy. Intrusive luxation of #8 at age 8, never treated.
patient.social_history: Pediatric patient accompanied by parent. High caries-risk diet but currently caries-free.
patient.chief_complaint: A bump on the gum above her front tooth. It doesn’t hurt.

clinical_findings.intraoral: Discolored #8 (gray). Labial sinus tract. Tooth slightly infraoccluded relative to #9. No mobility beyond physiologic.
clinical_findings.periodontal: PD 2–3 mm. No root fracture probing pattern.
clinical_findings.endodontic_testing: #8: no response to cold or EPT. Percussion negative. Palpation tender over the sinus tract. #7 and #9: normal responses.
clinical_findings.radiographs: PA/CBCT: #8 open apex (Cvek stage 4), thin dentinal walls, 8 mm apical rarefaction. No root fracture. Crown-root ratio currently acceptable.

flags: Immature necrotic tooth with apical periodontitis — regen vs MTA apexification
Thin walls → fracture risk if only a short MTA plug is placed without wall thickening
Sinus tract = chronic apical abscess
Growing patient — long-term restorability of a fragile root
guidelines: AAE Clinical Considerations for Regenerative Procedures (current)
IADT / AAE trauma follow-up; Cvek root-development stages

vignette.demographics: 10-year-old healthy girl. Intrusion of #8 at age 8, untreated.
vignette.chief: Asymptomatic labial gum bump above a gray front tooth.
vignette.clinical: Gray #8, labial sinus tract, slight infraocclusion. PD WNL.
vignette.endo: No cold/EPT response #8. Neighbors vital. Palpation tender over tract.
vignette.radio: Open apex, thin walls, 8 mm PA lesion. No fracture.

questions.q: The pulpal and apical diagnoses are:
options: Reversible pulpitis; normal apical tissues
Pulp necrosis; chronic apical abscess
Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis; acute apical abscess
Previously treated; asymptomatic apical periodontitis
questions.explanation: No response to cold/EPT plus a history of untreated intrusion = pulp necrosis. A sinus tract defines chronic apical abscess. Irreversible pulpitis requires a vital, lingering response. There is no swelling of acute abscess, and the tooth has not been treated. Reversible pulpitis does not produce necrosis or a sinus tract.

questions.q: The treatment option that best addresses both infection control AND future root-wall strength in this 10-year-old is:
options: Extraction and a Maryland bridge until implant age 18

Regenerative endodontic procedure (disinfection with low-concentration irrigant/medicament, evoked bleeding or biologic scaffold, coronal seal) as first-line to allow continued root development; MTA apexification as the evidence-based alternative if regen is not feasible
Standard gutta-percha obturation to the radiographic apex
Ca(OH)2 left in the canal until age 18 without a definitive seal
questions.explanation: For necrotic immature permanent teeth, the AAE positions regenerative endodontics as a first-line option because it uniquely offers the potential for increased root length/thickness and improved fracture resistance. MTA (or bioceramic) apexification predictably produces a barrier and high survival but does not thicken walls. GP cannot be condensed at an open apex and does not strengthen thin dentin. Indefinite Ca(OH)2 weakens dentin (long-term use associated with higher fracture risk). Extraction is a last resort in a 10-year-old given alveolar-growth and space-maintenance consequences; a Maryland bridge is a prosthetic backup, not the first endodontic choice for a restorable root.

title: Insufficient Ferrule after RCT on a Mandibular Molar
short: 55M • ASA II • #19 RCT • 1 mm remaining ferrule • Subgingival caries

patient.medical_history: Controlled hypertension.
patient.social_history: Former smoker, quit 10 years. Bruxism.
patient.chief_complaint: My dentist finished the root canal on my lower molar and said the remaining tooth is too short for a crown.

clinical_findings.intraoral: #19 endodontically treated, temporary restoration lost. Remaining axial walls: buccal 1 mm, lingual 0.5 mm, mesial 1 mm, distal caries to the bone crest. Gingival inflammation around the distal. Adjacent #18 and #20 intact. Opposing #14 is a crown.
clinical_findings.periodontal: PD 3 mm except 5 mm distal #19 with localized inflammation. Biologic width violation likely if a margin is placed at the current distal caries. Furcation not involved. Adequate bone height (~12 mm to the IAN on CBCT).
clinical_findings.occlusion: Group function. Moderate wear facets. Low smile line (molar not esthetic-critical).
clinical_findings.radiographs: Adequate RCT fill. Remaining dentin thin. Distal caries approximating crestal bone. Crown-root ratio currently ~1:1.5 if restored.

flags: Circumferential ferrule <2 mm (classic minimum 1.5–2 mm sound dentin)
Distal caries to crest → crown-lengthening would sacrifice bone/furcation
Bruxism increases catastrophic fracture risk of a ferrule-deficient post-core
Implant alternative is realistic in the posterior mandible
guidelines: Ferrule effect literature (Libman & Nicholls; 1.5–2 mm sound dentin)
GPT-10 definitions; crown-lengthening vs extrusion vs extract/implant decision analysis

vignette.demographics: 55-year-old male, ASA II, HTN. Former smoker. Bruxism.
vignette.chief: Recently completed RCT #19; remaining tooth structure judged inadequate for a crown.
vignette.clinical: Wall heights ≤1 mm; distal caries to crest. Localized distal PD 5 mm. Adjacent teeth intact. Low smile line.
vignette.endo: RCT appears technically adequate. No sinus tract. Percussion mildly tender while unrestored.
vignette.radio: Adequate fill. Distal caries to crestal bone. ~12 mm bone to IAN.

questions.q: The primary prosthodontic reason a conventional post-core and crown is high-risk here is:
options: The RCT fill is adequate, so no restoration is needed
Absence of a 1.5–2 mm circumferential ferrule of sound dentin, plus distal caries to crest and parafunction
Mandibular molars should never receive posts
The patient takes lisinopril, which contraindicates crowns
questions.explanation: The ferrule—1.5–2 mm of parallel, sound axial dentin engaged by the crown— is the dominant predictor of survival of endodontically treated teeth. Posts do not substitute for a ferrule. Distal caries to the crest means a restorative margin would violate biologic width unless crown lengthening or extrusion is performed; lengthening on a molar risks exposing the furcation. Bruxism multiplies fracture risk. Mandibular molars often don’t need posts if chamber retention exists, but that is secondary to the missing ferrule. Lisinopril is irrelevant.

questions.q: The most defensible treatment recommendation is:
options: Force a post-core and crown at the current gingival level and ‘watch the distal’
Surgical crown lengthening of 4 mm on the distal only, then a post-core, accepting furcation exposure
Present extraction of #19 with implant replacement (or a 3-unit FPD) versus orthodontic extrusion + crown lengthening to recapture ferrule—do not restore without a ferrule plan
A fiber post and core is uniquely able to eliminate the need for ferrule
questions.explanation: Restoring without a ferrule plan has a high rate of catastrophic root fracture, especially with parafunction. Distal-only aggressive lengthening on a molar commonly exposes the furcation and still may not yield 360° ferrule. Fiber posts do not create a ferrule. The ethical board-level plan is a shared decision: (1) extract and replace (implant is usually preferred to a 3-unit FPD if #18 and #20 are virgin), or (2) combined extrusion/lengthening if the patient is committed to saving the tooth and the remaining root is long enough. Either is defensible; ‘watch the distal’ is not.

title: Combination Syndrome — Maxillary CD vs Implant Overdenture
short: 68F • ASA II • Maxillary CD × 15 yrs • Mandibular Kennedy I

patient.medical_history: Osteoporosis on alendronate 70 mg weekly × 4 years (oral). Controlled HTN.
patient.social_history: Never smoker. Wears the maxillary denture 24 hours/day.
patient.chief_complaint: My upper denture drops when I talk, the front gums are getting bigger, and I only chew on my two lower front teeth.

clinical_findings.extraoral: Overclosed profile. Angular cheilitis.
clinical_findings.intraoral: Maxilla: flabby anterior ridge, papilla hyperplasia under the CD, posterior maxillary resorption with tuberosity hypertrophy. Mandible: remaining #22–27 with wear and super-eruption; bilateral posterior edentulism (Kennedy I); no RPD in use. Hyposalivation mild.
clinical_findings.occlusion: Only anterior occlusal contacts (combination-syndrome pattern). No posterior support.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Panoramic: severe posterior maxillary pneumatization; anterior maxillary residual ridge still has height but is mobile clinically. Mandibular anterior bone adequate. No MRONJ.

flags: Kelly combination syndrome pentad
Oral bisphosphonate × 4 years — implant consent/MRONJ risk (low but nonzero)
24-hour denture wear + inflammatory papillary hyperplasia
Need posterior mandibular support
guidelines: Kelly (1972) combination syndrome; GPT-10
McGill (2002) / York (2009) consensus — 2-implant mandibular overdenture as minimum standard vs CD
AAOMS 2022 MRONJ position paper (osteoporosis-dose oral BP)

vignette.demographics: 68-year-old female, ASA II. Oral alendronate × 4 years. HTN. 24-hour upper denture wear.
vignette.chief: Dropping upper denture, ‘growing’ front gums, chews only on lower front teeth.
vignette.clinical: Flabby anterior maxilla, papillary hyperplasia, hypertrophic tuberosities, mandibular Kennedy I with super-erupted worn anteriors, anterior-only occlusion, angular cheilitis.
vignette.endo: Mandibular anteriors vital, worn, no PA pathosis.
vignette.radio: Posterior maxillary pneumatization; mandibular anterior bone adequate; no MRONJ.

questions.q: The constellation of anterior maxillary bone/soft-tissue hyperplasia, posterior maxillary resorption, super-erupted mandibular anteriors, and lack of posterior occlusion is termed:
options: Eagle syndrome
Combination syndrome (Kelly)
Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Apertognathia from condylar degeneration
questions.explanation: Kelly’s combination syndrome describes the destructive pattern when a maxillary complete denture opposes mandibular anterior teeth without posterior support: flabby anterior maxilla, papillary hyperplasia, posterior maxillary resorption/tuberosity hypertrophy, extrusion of mandibular anteriors, and loss of OVD/posterior occlusion. Eagle syndrome is elongated styloid/pain. SJS is a mucocutaneous drug reaction. Condylar degeneration can cause open bite but not this maxillary-soft-tissue pattern.

questions.q: The rehabilitation strategy most likely to halt the syndrome and meet a contemporary minimum standard of care for the mandible is:
options: Relining the existing maxillary CD only
Extract remaining mandibular teeth and deliver a conventional mandibular CD (no implants) as first choice

Restore posterior mandibular support (ideally a 2-implant mandibular overdenture or implant-assisted RPD), a new maxillary CD (or implant-assisted maxillary prosthesis) after treating hyperplasia, and leave the denture out at night; discuss low MRONJ risk of implants on oral BP
Immediate maxillary zygomatic implants without addressing mandibular posterior support
questions.explanation: The driver is missing posterior mandibular support. McGill/York established the 2-implant mandibular overdenture as the minimum standard versus a conventional CD; an implant-assisted RPD is an alternative. A new maxillary CD after hyperplasia management (tissue rest, antifungal if needed, possible excision) and nocturnal denture removal are required. Relining alone does not restore posterior occlusion. Extracting healthy mandibular anteriors to make a conventional CD is regressive. Zygomatic implants without mandibular posterior support fail to treat the etiology. Oral bisphosphonates at osteoporosis doses are not an absolute implant contraindication per AAOMS 2022, but informed consent for MRONJ is mandatory.

title: Full-Arch Fixed Implant Rehabilitation — FP1 vs FP3 Selection
short: 59M • ASA II • Failing dentition • High smile line • Wants ‘teeth not gums’

patient.medical_history: T2DM HbA1c 6.8%. Former smoker, quit 4 years.
patient.social_history: Executive; high esthetic demand. Photographs show a high smile line with 3–4 mm of gingiva.
patient.chief_complaint: I want a fixed set of teeth that look like my own—not a denture with pink plastic.

clinical_findings.extraoral: High smile line. Medium lip support from failing maxillary incisors. Facial third otherwise balanced.
clinical_findings.intraoral: Generalized Stage IV periodontitis; multiple hopeless teeth. Current gingival levels of the maxillary incisors are near the planned incisal display, but extraction will cause 2–3+ mm of vertical ridge collapse in a thin buccal plate. Mandibular plane acceptable.
clinical_findings.radiographs: CBCT: maxillary anterior bone height 12–14 mm but buccal plate <1 mm. After extraction, restorative space from bone to planned incisal edge is 8–9 mm—inadequate for an FP3 pink prosthesis without reduction, but borderline for FP1 if tissues can be preserved.
clinical_findings.occlusion: Planning for mutually protected occlusion on a fixed complete arch.

flags: Patient requests FP1 (‘no pink’)
High smile line + thin buccal plate = high risk of black triangles/long teeth after extraction
Restorative space 8–9 mm may be insufficient for FP3 without ostectomy
HbA1c 6.8% acceptable for implants
guidelines: Misch/ITI prosthetic design FP1–FP3
Restorative space requirements: FP1 ≈ 8–12 mm; FP3 typically ≥12–15 mm from bone to incisal edge including acrylic/pink ceramic

vignette.demographics: 59-year-old male, ASA II. T2DM HbA1c 6.8%. Former smoker. High esthetic demand.
vignette.chief: Wants fixed teeth that look natural without visible pink prosthetic gingiva.
vignette.clinical: High smile line, Stage IV failing dentition, thin buccal plates, lip support currently from natural incisors.
vignette.endo: Multiple hopeless teeth; not candidates for retention.
vignette.radio: CBCT thin facial bone. Restorative space bone-to-incisal ≈8–9 mm if no ostectomy.

questions.q: An FP1 (tooth-only, no prosthetic gingiva) restoration is esthetically realistic here only if:
options: The patient has a high smile line—FP1 is always easier with a high smile
Soft- and hard-tissue architecture (papillae, mid-facial contours) can be preserved or reconstructed to the level of the adjacent gingival zeniths; otherwise long teeth/black triangles will show
FP1 requires at least 18 mm of restorative space
Diabetes precludes FP3, so FP1 is mandatory
questions.explanation: FP1 mimics natural teeth and requires the residual or reconstructed tissues to sit at a natural gingival level. A high smile line exposes any tissue deficiency, making FP1 harder—not easier. If extraction collapse is expected (thin plates), an FP2/FP3 with prosthetic gingiva hidden under the lip, or staged grafting/delayed FP1, must be discussed. FP3 needs more restorative space (often 12–15+ mm), not FP1. Diabetes at HbA1c 6.8% does not dictate prosthetic classification.

questions.q: Given 8–9 mm of bone-to-incisal space and a high smile line, the most honest pretreatment counseling is:
options: Guarantee an FP1 with immediate load today

Explain that extraction collapse may force either (a) grafting/staged FP1 or (b) ostectomy plus FP3 with a flange designed to stay under the lip; a try-in / digital smile design is required before committing
Always reduce 8 mm of bone so that FP3 acrylic can be packed
A maxillary complete denture is the only predictable esthetic option
questions.explanation: Restorative space, smile line, and ridge collapse risk must be prototyped (DSD, mock-up, provisional) before promising a prosthetic class. Automatic ostectomy to create FP3 space is irreversible and may be unnecessary if grafting/preservation can support FP1—or undesirable if the patient refuses pink. A CD is an alternative, not the only option. Immediate-load FP1 without a tissue plan is a common source of esthetic failure.

title: Localized Anterior Tooth Wear — Dahl Concept vs Full-Mouth Rehabilitation
short: 34M • ASA I • Palatal erosion #6–11 • Unopposed during protrusion

patient.medical_history: GERD, now treated with PPI. History of a high-acid energy-drink habit (stopped 1 year ago).
patient.social_history: Software engineer; no bruxism appliance. Never smoker.
patient.chief_complaint: My upper front teeth look thinner and feel sharp on the tongue side. I don’t want my whole mouth crowned.

clinical_findings.extraoral: Normal facial thirds. No TMD pain. Canine-guided occlusion remaining but palatal concavities on #6–11.
clinical_findings.intraoral: Cupped palatal erosion confined to maxillary anteriors. Incisal edges of #8–9 shortened 1 mm with translucent rims. Posterior occlusal contacts currently present in MIP (localized wear, not generalized). Mandibular incisors mild compensatory eruption. Saliva adequate now that GERD is treated.
clinical_findings.occlusion: MIP stable posteriorly. Anterior coupling lost on protrusion because of palatal substance loss. No posterior wear facets of significance.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Vital pulps; remaining palatal dentin on #8–9 ≈1.2 mm clinically over the pulp horns. No PA pathosis.

flags: Localized (not generalized) erosive wear
GERD now controlled — disease control before reconstruction
Dahl / palatal additive composite or ceramic to regain guidance
Avoid full-mouth crowns in a 34-year-old with intact posteriors
guidelines: European consensus on erosive tooth wear (BEWE); additive prosthodontics / Dahl principle
GPT-10: occlusal vertical dimension — do not increase VDO without a reason

vignette.demographics: 34-year-old healthy male. Treated GERD. Prior acidic drinks. ASA I.
vignette.chief: Thin, sharp palatal surfaces of upper front teeth; wants conservative care.
vignette.clinical: Localized palatal erosion #6–11, 1 mm incisal shortening, posteriors intact in MIP, mild compensatory eruption of lower incisors.
vignette.endo: All anteriors vital. Thin remaining palatal dentin over pulp horns of #8–9.
vignette.radio: No PA lesions. Pulp horns close to palatal surfaces.

questions.q: The most conservative, evidence-congruent plan to restore palatal anatomy and incisal guidance is:
options: Full-mouth crown rehabilitation at a 4 mm increased VDO

Additive palatal restorations (bonded composite or thin ceramic) using a Dahl-type local occlusal appliance/build-up so that posteriors re-erupt into contact over weeks–months, after confirming GERD control
Elective RCT and posts on #6–11 because dentin is thin
Extract #7–10 and place a 4-unit implant FPD
questions.explanation: Localized anterior erosive wear with intact posterior MIP is a classic Dahl indication: palatal additive restorations create a small posterior open bite that closes by relative eruption/intrusion over 3–6 months, restoring guidance without crowning the entire dentition or arbitrarily raising VDO 4 mm. Disease control (PPI, diet) must precede reconstruction. Elective RCT is unjustified on vital teeth; if pulp proximity is critical, a very conservative additive approach or a delayed ceramic after a composite trial is used. Extraction/implants are grossly aggressive.

questions.q: A 4 mm arbitrary increase in OVD with full-coverage crowns would be inappropriate primarily because:
options: OVD can never be changed in adults
There is no generalized wear, loss of posterior support, or prosthetic space problem requiring a full-mouth OVD change
GERD patients are not candidates for bonded ceramics
The Dahl concept is obsolete and banned
questions.explanation: OVD can be altered when needed (full-mouth wear, restorative space, airway appliances), but it is not a goal in itself. This patient has localized wear and existing posterior contacts; a 4 mm full-mouth reconstruction is overtreatment. Bonded ceramics/composites are acceptable after acid control. The Dahl principle remains a valid, conservative tool for localized anterior wear.

title: Mandibular Implant Overdenture — Locator vs Bar, McGill/York
short: 72M • ASA III • New complete edentulism • Loose lower denture

patient.medical_history: CAD with stent 3 years ago (on aspirin 81 mg). Mild COPD. HbA1c 6.9%.
patient.social_history: Former smoker (quit 6 years). Lives independently. Limited income (VA/DoD beneficiary). Cannot tolerate a mandibular CD.
patient.chief_complaint: The lower denture floats and I cannot eat steak or salad. The upper denture is acceptable.

clinical_findings.intraoral: Maxillary CD well-retained (favorable palate). Mandibular residual ridge Atwood class IV (severely resorbed). Floor of mouth attachments high. Adequate interarch space (>12 mm from ridge to maxillary plane). Saliva slightly reduced.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Panoramic/CBCT: 12 mm bone height in the interforaminal region, adequate width for standard implants. Mental foramina relatively anterior. Posterior bone 6–8 mm to the IAN.
clinical_findings.occlusion: Current CDs have worn monoplane teeth and reduced OVD.

flags: McGill/York: 2-implant overdenture is minimum standard vs mandibular CD
Interforaminal 12 mm height — 2 implants feasible
Aspirin monotherapy — typically continue for implant surgery
Bar vs unsplinted locators: hygiene, cost, parallelism, ridge height
guidelines: McGill Consensus 2002; York Consensus 2009
ITI overdenture protocols; AHA — continue aspirin for most dental surgery

vignette.demographics: 72-year-old male, ASA III. CAD on aspirin, COPD, T2DM HbA1c 6.9%. Former smoker. Cannot wear a lower CD.
vignette.chief: Floating mandibular denture; maxillary CD acceptable.
vignette.clinical: Atwood IV mandibular ridge, high floor-of-mouth attachments, >12 mm interarch space, favorable maxillary denture foundation.
vignette.radio: Interforaminal height 12 mm, adequate width; mental foramina anterior; posterior height 6–8 mm.

questions.q: Based on the McGill and York consensus statements, the minimum standard of care to offer this patient for the mandible is:
options: A new conventional mandibular complete denture only, because of ASA III status
A two-implant mandibular overdenture (unsplinted or splinted)
A full-arch fixed FP3 prosthesis on 6 implants as the minimum
Soft-liner replacements every 8 weeks indefinitely
questions.explanation: McGill (2002) and York (2009) state that a 2-implant mandibular overdenture should be the minimum offered to edentulous patients, not a conventional CD alone. ASA III is not a contraindication when diabetes is controlled and CAD is stable; it is a reason for medical consultation and simplified surgery (2 interforaminal implants), not denial of care. A 6-implant FP3 may be excellent but is not the ‘minimum standard’ and is more costly/surgical. Soft liners are palliative.

questions.q: For a resorbed ridge with limited income and fair hygiene, the most practical attachment design is usually:
options: Unsplinted stud attachments (e.g., Locator-type) on two non-angulated implants, accepting slightly less stability than a bar in exchange for hygiene, repairability, and cost
A milled bar with distal cantilevers to replace posterior teeth without a denture flange
Four zygomatic implants
Magnets only, because aspirin users cannot receive stud attachments
questions.explanation: Two unsplinted stud attachments are the workhorse McGill-type design: lower cost, easier hygiene, and straightforward maintenance. Bars can help with highly resorbed ridges and nonparallel implants but cost more and complicate hygiene. Distal cantilevers on a bar do not convert an overdenture into a fixed prosthesis and can overload implants. Zygomatic implants are a maxillary tool. Aspirin has no bearing on attachment type; it is typically continued for the surgery itself.

title: Stage 2 MRONJ and a Cracked Mandibular Molar on Alendronate
short: 71F • ASA III • Alendronate 8 yrs • Exposed bone #30 region

patient.medical_history: Osteoporosis on alendronate 70 mg weekly × 8 years (cumulative oral BP exposure high). No cancer, no IV bisphosphonates, no denosumab, no radiation. T2DM HbA1c 7.2%.
patient.social_history: Never smoker.
patient.chief_complaint: A piece of bone is sticking out behind my lower right molar and it has been sore and draining for 6 weeks. The tooth cracked last year but I declined treatment.

clinical_findings.extraoral: No cutaneous fistula. No neurosensory deficit. Mild right submandibular tenderness.
clinical_findings.intraoral: Exposed yellowish bone 4 × 3 mm on the lingual shelf distal to #30. #30 has a split crown, probing to the apex on the lingual, pus expressed. Adjacent mucosa erythematous. No extraoral swelling.
clinical_findings.radiographs: PA/CBCT: #30 VRF with J-shaped radiolucency. Mixed sclerotic/lytic bone at the lingual cortex distal to #30. Inferior border intact. No pathologic fracture.

flags: AAOMS Stage 2 MRONJ: exposed bone >8 weeks + infection/pain, on antiresorptive, no radiation
Oral osteoporosis-dose BP × 8 years
Stage 3 would require pathologic fracture, extraoral fistula, or osteolysis to inferior border
CTX is NOT recommended as a decision tool (AAOMS 2022)
guidelines: AAOMS 2022 Position Paper on Medication-Related Osteonecrosis of the Jaw
Do not use serum CTX as a sole extraction-risk predictor

vignette.demographics: 71-year-old female, ASA III. Oral alendronate × 8 years for osteoporosis. T2DM HbA1c 7.2%. Never smoker. No IV BP, denosumab, or radiation.
vignette.chief: Painful exposed bone and drainage for 6 weeks distal to a cracked lower right molar.
vignette.clinical: 4×3 mm exposed lingual bone distal to #30; split #30 with a lingual probe-to-apex and pus. No extraoral fistula, no lip numbness.
vignette.radio: J-shaped lesion #30; mixed sclerosis/lysis of lingual cortex; inferior border intact.

questions.q: The AAOMS 2022 stage of MRONJ is:
options: Stage 0 (nonspecific symptoms, no exposed bone)
Stage 1 (exposed bone, asymptomatic, no infection)
Stage 2 (exposed bone with pain/infection)
Stage 3 (exposed bone plus pathologic fracture, extraoral fistula, or osteolysis to the inferior border)
questions.explanation: Stage 2 is exposed/necrotic bone in a patient on antiresorptive/antiangiogenic therapy (and no radiation) with pain and infection (erythema, purulence). Stage 0 has no exposed bone. Stage 1 is exposed bone without infection/pain. Stage 3 requires more extensive disease (pathologic fracture, extraoral fistula, nasal/antral communication, osteolysis to the inferior border, or neurosensory involvement from the necrosis). The inferior border is intact and there is no extraoral fistula, so this is Stage 2, not 3.

questions.q: The most appropriate management of #30 and the MRONJ is:
options: Refuse all treatment until a CTX value is ‘above 150 pg/mL’

Chlorhexidine rinses, targeted antimicrobial therapy, and conservative sequestrectomy/extraction of the VRF tooth with smooth bony contouring of exposed sharp edges; coordinate a possible drug holiday with the prescribing physician (evidence is inconclusive)
Aggressive wide resection to bleeding bone and immediate reconstruction plate as first-line Stage 2 therapy
Hyperbaric oxygen as mandatory monotherapy
questions.explanation: AAOMS 2022 Stage 2 care is infection control (antimicrobials, CHX) plus conservative debridement/sequestrectomy to reduce sharp exposed bone; removal of the causative hopeless tooth is indicated and is not ‘elective cosmetic extraction.’ CTX is explicitly not recommended as a binary decision tool. Wide resection is reserved for Stage 3 or refractory disease. HBO is not mandatory first-line for MRONJ (more established as an adjunct in osteoradionecrosis protocols). Drug holidays remain of unproven benefit and must be decided with the physician, balancing fracture risk.

title: High-Risk IAN Relationship of #32 — Coronectomy vs Extraction
short: 24M • ASA I • Recurrent pericoronitis #32 • Canal grooving on CBCT

patient.medical_history: Noncontributory. Two episodes of pericoronitis #32 in 6 months, one with trismus.
patient.social_history: College student. Never smoker.
patient.chief_complaint: My wisdom tooth keeps getting infected. I want it out before I leave for a field assignment.

clinical_findings.intraoral: Partially erupted, mesioangular #32 with an operculum. No current abscess. #17 similarly impacted but asymptomatic. Tongue/lip sensation intact (baseline documented).
clinical_findings.radiographs: Panoramic: Rood & Shehab signs — darkening of the root, interruption of the white line of the canal at #32. CBCT: IAN in a buccal groove of the middle third of the root; loss of cortication; root dilaceration. No cystic change.

flags: Recurrent pericoronitis = indication for removal
CBCT high-risk IAN: grooving + loss of cortication
Coronectomy indicated when the risk of IAN injury outweighs the risk of retained roots
Document neurosensory baseline
guidelines: AAOMS third-molar management; coronectomy evidence (Renton et al.)
CBCT when panoramic high-risk signs are present

vignette.demographics: 24-year-old healthy male. Recurrent pericoronitis #32. Upcoming field assignment.
vignette.chief: Wants #32 extracted after two pericoronitis episodes.
vignette.clinical: Partially erupted mesioangular #32, currently uninfected. Baseline lip/tongue sensation intact.
vignette.radio: Panoramic high-risk Rood signs. CBCT: IAN grooving the root with loss of cortication; dilaceration.

questions.q: The imaging finding that most strongly predicts IAN injury with complete extraction is:
options: Mesioangular position alone
CBCT-demonstrated grooving/interruption of the canal cortices by the root
The fact that the tooth is partially erupted
A 24-year-old patient age
questions.explanation: Panoramic Rood & Shehab signs prompt CBCT. On CBCT, loss of canal cortication and grooving/perforation of the root by the IAN are the highest-risk anatomic relationships. Angulation, eruption status, and age influence difficulty and PDL maturity but do not by themselves equal the nerve-injury prediction of a grooved canal.

questions.q: The most appropriate surgical recommendation is:
options: Coronectomy (intentional retention of roots) with informed consent about possible second surgery if roots migrate, because complete extraction carries a high IAN-injury risk and the tooth is otherwise sound (no caries into the root, no associated cyst/tumor)
Aggressive complete extraction at all costs because coronectomy is experimental
Operculectomy only, which cures recurrent pericoronitis
No treatment; pericoronitis is not an indication for surgery
questions.explanation: Coronectomy is an accepted option when CBCT shows a high-risk IAN relationship, the roots are not mobile/diseased, and there is no associated cyst/caries into the retained fragment. It substantially reduces IAN deficit rates. Consent must include root migration (~2–6 mm often) and possible later retrieval (usually safer once the nerve relationship improves). Complete extraction remains acceptable if the patient declines coronectomy after risk discussion, but ‘at all costs’ is not required. Operculectomy fails in recurrent mesioangular impactions. Recurrent pericoronitis is a classic indication to treat before a field assignment (see also DRC-003).

title: Non-Healing Floor-of-Mouth Ulcer — Biopsy Decision Tree
short: 58M • ASA II • 40 pack-years • Ulcer 8 weeks • Indurated

patient.medical_history: COPD. Hypertension. No prior malignancy.
patient.social_history: 40 pack-year smoker, still smoking. 6 beers/day. Construction worker.
patient.chief_complaint: A sore under my tongue that hasn’t healed since I chipped a filling two months ago. My dentist smoothed the filling, but the sore is still there and my tongue feels thick.

clinical_findings.extraoral: Left level IB lymph node 1.5 cm, firm, mobile, nontender. No trismus.
clinical_findings.intraoral: 2.5 × 1.5 cm ulcer on the left floor of mouth extending onto the ventral tongue. Rolled, indurated borders. Does not wipe off. Adjacent #19 amalgam recently smoothed; no remaining sharp edge. Reduced tongue mobility. Neck exam as above.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Panoramic: no odontogenic source. Consider CT/MRI staging after tissue diagnosis—do not delay biopsy for imaging if cancer is suspected, but imaging should be obtained promptly.

flags: Ulcer >2 weeks (here 8 weeks) with induration in a high-risk patient = cancer until proven otherwise
Tobacco + alcohol synergy
Firm cervical node
Do NOT treat empirically with silver nitrate / prolonged steroids instead of biopsy
guidelines: NCCN Head and Neck Cancers; ADA oral-cancer detection
Any non-healing ulcer >14 days requires tissue diagnosis; incisional biopsy of the margin/most representative area

vignette.demographics: 58-year-old male, ASA II. 40 pack-years, 6 beers/day, COPD, HTN.
vignette.chief: Floor-of-mouth ulcer 8 weeks after a chipped filling; filling was smoothed; lesion persists; tongue feels thick.
vignette.clinical: 2.5 cm indurated FOM/ventral-tongue ulcer, rolled borders, reduced tongue mobility, firm 1.5 cm level IB node. No remaining sharp dental source.

questions.q: The most appropriate next step is:
options: Prescribe nystatin and re-evaluate in 6 weeks
Incisional biopsy of the ulcer margin (and urgent head-and-neck oncology / OMFS referral); do not wait another 2-week ‘trial of smoothing’
Excisional biopsy of the entire 2.5 cm lesion and the lymph node in a dental operatory under local anesthesia
Silver nitrate cautery of the ulcer
questions.explanation: A non-healing indurated ulcer >2 weeks in a high-risk (tobacco/alcohol) site (floor of mouth) is oral squamous-cell carcinoma until proven otherwise. Incisional biopsy of the representative margin provides diagnosis without compromising later oncologic resection. Complete office excision of a 2.5 cm FOM lesion plus a node is not appropriate—the patient needs staging (CT/MRI ± PET) and a multidisciplinary cancer operation with margins and neck management. Antifungals address candidiasis that wipes off; this lesion is indurated and does not wipe off. Cautery destroys tissue and delays diagnosis.

questions.q: The firm 1.5 cm level IB node most likely represents:
options: A reactive node that rules out malignancy
Possible regional metastasis; it supports urgency but does not replace tissue diagnosis of the primary
Proof of lymphoma rather than SCC
An indication to start empiric antibiotics for 30 days
questions.explanation: Level IB is the first-echelon drainage of the floor of mouth. A firm node in this setting is metastatic SCC until staging proves otherwise. It increases urgency and will be addressed by the oncology team (neck dissection or CRT per NCCN), but the primary still needs biopsy. A reactive node is possible but cannot be assumed. Lymphoma is far less likely given a classic mucosal SCC phenotype. Antibiotics delay care.

title: Odontogenic Deep-Space Infection with Floor-of-Mouth Elevation
short: 27M • ASA I • #17 pericoronitis • Trismus 12 mm • ‘Hot potato’ voice

patient.medical_history: Healthy. 48 hours of worsening swelling after a failed course of oral penicillin from an urgent-care clinic.
patient.medications: Penicillin VK (non-adherent after 4 doses because he could not swallow).
patient.social_history: Never smoker.
patient.chief_complaint: I can’t open my mouth, I’m drooling, and my tongue feels pushed up. It’s hard to breathe when I lie down.

clinical_findings.vital_signs: T 38.7°C, HR 118, BP 128/78, RR 22, SpO2 96% sitting, 92% supine. Toxic appearance.
clinical_findings.extraoral: Bilateral submandibular swelling, more left. Firm floor of mouth. Tongue elevated and posteriorly displaced. ‘Hot potato’ voice. Trismus: 12 mm. No fluctuance extraorally yet.
clinical_findings.intraoral: Cannot visualize the oropharynx well. Operculum #17 with pus. Floor of mouth tense and elevated.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Do not send an unstable airway patient to a distant CT scanner unaccompanied. Once the airway is secured or deemed stable by a capable team, contrast CT of the neck maps spaces.

flags: Ludwig angina spectrum — bilateral submandibular + sublingual elevation
Airway first (ABC)
Trismus + drooling + positional desaturation = emergency
Source control after airway/antibiotics — not oral penicillin at home
guidelines: AAOMS / head-neck infection principles: airway, IV empiric antibiotics covering mixed oral flora/MRSA per local antibiogram, prompt incision and drainage, source removal
Ludwig angina is a clinical diagnosis

vignette.demographics: 27-year-old healthy male. Failed outpatient penicillin. Rapidly progressive swelling from #17.
vignette.chief: Trismus, drooling, elevated tongue, orthopnea.
vignette.clinical: Febrile, tachycardic, SpO2 drop supine. Bilateral submandibular swelling, tense elevated floor of mouth, hot-potato voice, 12 mm trismus, pus at #17 operculum.
vignette.radio: Defer imaging until airway is secure.

questions.q: The first priority is:
options: A 10-day prescription of oral amoxicillin–clavulanate and follow-up next week

Immediate airway assessment/management (sitting position, prepare for fiberoptic/awake intubation or surgical airway) in a setting capable of emergency surgical airway, then IV antibiotics and drainage
Hot salt-water rinses and extraction of #17 in a general-practice chair with 2% lidocaine only
CT first in an unmonitored outpatient imaging center before any treatment
questions.explanation: This is a threatened airway (elevated tongue, hot-potato voice, drooling, desaturation when supine). Airway management in a controlled OR/ED setting precedes everything. Oral antibiotics and delayed follow-up are how Ludwig angina becomes fatal. Office extraction under local with 12 mm trismus is unsafe. Unmonitored CT can lose the airway in the scanner. After airway security: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and urgent I&D plus removal of #17.

questions.q: This presentation is best described as:
options: Simple vestibular abscess
Ludwig angina (rapidly spreading bilateral submandibular/sublingual cellulitis) until proven otherwise
Peritonsillar abscess as the primary diagnosis
Angioedema from penicillin
questions.explanation: Ludwig angina is aggressive bilateral infection of the submandibular and sublingual spaces with tongue elevation and airway risk, usually odontogenic (mandibular molars / 3rd molars). A vestibular abscess is localized. Peritonsillar abscess presents with uvular deviation and sore throat without this floor-of-mouth board-like swelling. Penicillin angioedema lacks fever/pus/source tooth. Treat as Ludwig until the airway is safe and imaging/surgical findings refine the spaces involved.

title: Atrophic Edentulous Mandible — Preprosthetic Risk of Fracture
short: 78F • ASA III • Atwood VI mandible • Fractured denture • Wants implants

patient.medical_history: Osteoporosis (denosumab 60 mg q6mo × 3 years). CAD. Hypothyroidism.
patient.social_history: Never smoker. Independent living. Cannot wear the lower denture after a midline fracture of the prosthesis.
patient.chief_complaint: My lower jaw feels thin. I want ‘snaps’ for a new denture. My sister had a jaw fracture after implants.

clinical_findings.intraoral: Pencil-thin mandibular residual ridge. Mental foramina on the ridge crest (dysesthesia with the denture). Maxillary CD acceptable.
clinical_findings.radiographs: CBCT: anterior mandibular height 7 mm, width 5–6 mm of dense cortex with almost no marrow. Posterior height 5 mm above the IAN. No MRONJ currently.

flags: Atwood VI / 7 mm height — pathologic fracture risk with implant osteotomy
Denosumab (RANKL inhibitor) — MRONJ risk higher than oral BP; elective implants controversial
Mental nerve on the crest
Short implants vs grafting vs short-span overdenture vs no surgery
guidelines: AAOMS 2022 MRONJ — denosumab implants not routinely recommended especially in atrophic jaws
Preprosthetic surgery: fracture risk when height <8–10 mm for conventional implants

vignette.demographics: 78-year-old female, ASA III. Denosumab for osteoporosis × 3 years. CAD on aspirin. Pencil-thin mandible.
vignette.chief: Wants implant ‘snaps’ for a lower denture; family history of jaw fracture after implants.
vignette.clinical: Atwood VI ridge, mental nerves on the crest, maxillary CD OK.
vignette.radio: Anterior height 7 mm, width 5–6 mm cortical; posterior 5 mm above IAN.

questions.q: The greatest surgical risk of placing standard interforaminal implants in this 7 mm mandible is:
options: Sinus perforation
Iatrogenic pathologic fracture of the atrophic mandible
Anosmia
Lingual nerve anesthesia as the most likely deficit
questions.explanation: Atrophic mandibles (<8–10 mm) are at documented risk of fracture during or after implant osteotomy because the remaining bone is a cortical tube. Sinus perforation is a maxillary issue. Olfaction is unrelated. The mental nerve (not lingual) is at risk here because the foramina sit on the crest; lingual nerve is a third-molar concern.

questions.q: The most defensible recommendation is:
options: Four 15 mm implants with bicortical engagement this week while holding denosumab
