Candid counseling that elective implants are relatively contraindicated on denosumab in an atrophic mandible (MRONJ + fracture); offer a well-made conventional CD/soft liner, or, if implants are still pursued, coordinate oncology/endocrine-level risk discussion, possible delayed timing around denosumab, short/mini implants or grafting in a center equipped for fracture, with written informed consent
Immediate iliac-crest reconstruction as routine dental care
Ignore denosumab because it is not a bisphosphonate
questions.explanation: Denosumab is a potent antiresorptive with well-documented MRONJ, including after implants; AAOMS does not treat it as ‘safer than bisphosphonates.’ Combined with a 7 mm mandible, elective implant surgery is high-risk. A conventional prosthesis is the safest default. If the patient still requests implants, this is a specialist shared decision (drug timing, fracture-ready OR, short implants vs augmentation), not a routine two-locator case. Denosumab’s mechanism (RANKL) is different from BP but the MRONJ risk is real and may persist after discontinuation (rebound vertebral fractures complicate holidays).

title: Acute Closed Lock — Disc Displacement without Reduction with Limited Opening
short: 34F • ASA II • Clicking stopped 3 days ago • Opening 24 mm

patient.medical_history: Generalized anxiety disorder on sertraline 50 mg daily. No systemic arthritis.
patient.social_history: Never smoker. High-stress occupation. History of gum chewing.
patient.chief_complaint: Clicking in my right jaw for two years, but three days ago the clicking stopped and now I can barely open my mouth.

clinical_findings.extraoral: No facial swelling. Right TMJ tender to lateral pole palpation. Masseter and temporalis tender.
clinical_findings.range_of_motion: Unassisted opening 24 mm with deflection to the right. Passive stretch 28 mm with a hard end-feel. Right laterotrusion 4 mm; left laterotrusion 9 mm. No current click (click historically present).
clinical_findings.intraoral: Dentition intact. No acute occlusal change. Wear consistent with clenching.
clinical_findings.imaging: CBCT: normal condylar cortical morphology bilaterally; reduced translation of the right condyle on open view. MRI (if obtained): anteriorly displaced right disc without reduction.

flags: Sudden loss of click + limited opening <40 mm + ipsilateral deflection = DDWOR with limited opening
Hard end-feel
Normal CBCT cortex → not primarily DJD
Axis I diagnosis first; do not equilibrate or crown at this visit
guidelines: DC/TMD Axis I (Schiffman et al. 2014) — disc displacement without reduction with limited opening
AAOP / ICOP — acute closed lock management is conservative/minimally invasive first

vignette.demographics: 34-year-old female, ASA II. GAD on sertraline. Two-year reciprocal click.
vignette.chief: Clicking stopped 3 days ago; severe limited opening.
vignette.clinical: Unassisted opening 24 mm, passive 28 mm hard end-feel, deflection to the right. Right TMJ and elevator-muscle tenderness. No current click.
vignette.endo: No odontogenic source. All posterior teeth vital if tested.
vignette.radio: CBCT: normal cortices, limited right translation. MRI would show ADD without reduction.

questions.q: According to DC/TMD Axis I, the primary right TMJ diagnosis is:
options: Disc displacement with reduction
Disc displacement without reduction with limited opening
Degenerative joint disease (osteoarthritis)
Subluxation of the temporomandibular joint
questions.explanation: DC/TMD DD without reduction with limited opening requires: (1) a history of TMJ noise that stopped AND jaw locking, and (2) maximum assisted opening including overbite <40 mm. Sudden cessation of a reciprocal click with opening of 24–28 mm and deflection toward the affected side is the classic acute closed lock. DD with reduction would still click and would not limit opening this severely. DJD requires crepitus plus imaging of degeneration (CBCT cortices are normal). Subluxation is hypermobility with an open lock, the opposite of this presentation.

questions.q: The most appropriate immediate management is:
options: Irreversible occlusal equilibration and four-unit anterior crowns to ‘capture the disc’

Education, soft diet, NSAIDs as tolerated, jaw-mobilization/physical therapy, and a short-term anterior-repositioning or stabilizing appliance as indicated; arthrocentesis if it fails to unlock in a timely manner
Bilateral TMJ replacement this week
Mandatory MRI before any palliative care
questions.explanation: Acute closed lock is managed conservatively first: explanation, anti-inflammatory measures, physiotherapy/manual mobilization, and a reversible appliance. Many reduce in days to weeks. Arthrocentesis is the next minimally invasive step for persistent lock/pain. Irreversible occlusal treatment and total joint replacement are not first-line. MRI is useful if surgery is contemplated or the diagnosis is unclear, but it is not required before starting conservative care in a classic DC/TMD presentation.

title: Myofascial Pain with Referral Mimicking Irreversible Pulpitis
short: 41F • ASA I • ‘Toothache’ #3 • All endo tests normal

patient.medical_history: Migraine, well controlled. No sinus disease diagnosed.
patient.social_history: Parafunction (daytime clenching at a computer). Never smoker.
patient.chief_complaint: My upper right molar is killing me. Two dentists said it might need a root canal, but the x-rays look fine.

clinical_findings.endodontic_testing: #2, #3, #4: normal cold without lingering, EPT WNL, no percussion/palpation tenderness, no sinus tract. Bite test negative. No cracked-tooth findings.
clinical_findings.tmd_exam: Right deep masseter trigger point: palpation reproduces the familiar ‘tooth’ pain to #3 (referral). Temporalis anterior also refers to the maxilla. Unassisted opening 44 mm without deflection. No joint click. Palpation of TMJ poles non-tender.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Bitewing/PA/sinus PA: no caries, no PA rarefaction, no sinus OPACITY of acute sinusitis. CBCT not indicated at this step.

flags: Endodontically normal tooth + masseter referral = myofascial pain with referral (DC/TMD)
Do not RCT a vital, non-pathologic tooth
ICOP distinguishes TMD-related pain from odontogenic pain
Axis II screen (PHQ-4, GCPS) still indicated
guidelines: DC/TMD: myalgia vs myofascial pain with referral
AAE: do not treat pulp based on pain referral without confirming pulpal diagnosis

vignette.demographics: 41-year-old healthy female. Migraine history. Daytime clenching.
vignette.chief: Perceived toothache #3; prior recommendation for RCT; radiographs ‘fine’.
vignette.clinical: Normal endodontic testing all maxillary right posteriors. Right masseter trigger point reproduces the exact tooth pain. Opening 44 mm, joints non-tender, no click.
vignette.radio: No caries, no PA lesion, no acute sinus findings.

questions.q: The DC/TMD muscle diagnosis that best fits is:
options: Local myalgia only (pain stays under the palpating finger)
Myofascial pain with referral (familiar pain referred to the tooth on palpation of the masseter)
Arthralgia of the right TMJ
Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis of #3
questions.explanation: Myofascial pain with referral is familiar pain that spreads beyond the palpated muscle. Reproduction of the chief ‘toothache’ by masseter palpation is diagnostic. Local myalgia remains under the finger. Arthralgia requires joint-line pain modified by jaw movement and joint palpation—the poles are non-tender here. Irreversible pulpitis requires a lingering pulpal response and is excluded by normal sensibility testing and pristine radiographs.

questions.q: The most appropriate next treatment is:
options: RCT and a crown on #3 today
Education, parafunction awareness, physical therapy/self-care, and a trial of a stabilizing appliance; avoid irreversible dental treatment
Extraction of #3 because referral means the tooth is necrotic
Empiric antibiotics for occult sinusitis
questions.explanation: Once odontogenic pathosis is ruled out, management is conservative TMD care. RCT or extraction of a normal tooth is a classic and preventable error. Antibiotics have no role without infection. If the pain later localizes with a true pulpal change, the endodontic diagnosis can be revisited—but not before.

title: Degenerative Joint Disease with Crepitus and Headache Attributed to TMD
short: 58F • ASA II • Grinding crepitus • Morning headache • OA knees

patient.medical_history: Primary osteoarthritis of the knees. No rheumatoid arthritis. Perimenopausal.
patient.medications: Acetaminophen PRN; no chronic NSAID because of GERD.
patient.social_history: Never smoker. Reports sleep grinding.
patient.chief_complaint: My left jaw sounds like gravel, and I wake up with a temple headache that gets worse when I chew.

clinical_findings.range_of_motion: Opening 38 mm with slight deflection to the left. Crepitus (coarse) on the left TMJ during opening/closing, confirmed with stethoscope. Left TMJ lateral-pole pain familiar to the patient. Masseter tenderness mild.
clinical_findings.occlusion: Stable MIP. Left posterior wear. No acute open bite.
clinical_findings.imaging: CBCT: left condylar flattening, subchondral sclerosis, and a small subchondral cyst; osteophyte on the anterior condyle. Right condyle mild flattening only. Joint space reduced on the left.

flags: DC/TMD DJD = crepitus + bony changes on CBCT
Arthralgia can coexist
Headache attributed to TMD (ICOP) if familiar headache is reproduced by TMD provocation
GERD limits NSAIDs
guidelines: DC/TMD degenerative joint disease criteria
ICOP — headache attributed to TMD; AAOP conservative OA care first

vignette.demographics: 58-year-old female with knee OA and GERD. Sleep bruxism.
vignette.chief: Left ‘gravel’ jaw noise and morning temple headache worse with chewing.
vignette.clinical: Opening 38 mm, left coarse crepitus, left joint-line familiar pain, mild masseter tenderness.
vignette.endo: Teeth vital; headache is not a toothache.
vignette.radio: CBCT left condyle: flattening, sclerosis, osteophyte, subchondral cyst.

questions.q: The left TMJ osseous diagnosis by DC/TMD is:
options: Disc displacement with reduction without imaging, because crepitus equals a click
Degenerative joint disease (confirmed by crepitus plus CBCT bony change)
Synovial chondromatosis as the most likely diagnosis
Normal TMJ
questions.explanation: DC/TMD DJD is diagnosed by crepitus (or imaging alone in some research criteria) plus radiographic degeneration (flattening, sclerosis, osteophytes, cysts, erosion). A click is a discrete pop of DDWR, not coarse gravel crepitus. Synovial chondromatosis is rare and shows loose bodies. The joint is not normal on CBCT.

questions.q: First-line therapy for painful TMJ DJD in this patient is:
options: Total joint replacement as the initial step for any osteophyte

Conservative care: education, self-care, physical therapy, a stabilizing night appliance for bruxism, and analgesia compatible with GERD (acetaminophen ± short topical NSAID / physician-guided options); arthrocentesis if pain persists
Full-mouth reconstruction to a neuromuscular ‘centric’
Long-term high-dose oral ketorolac despite GERD
questions.explanation: Painful TMJ OA is treated like other synovial joints: load reduction, PT, reversible appliances, and analgesia. TJR is for end-stage disease with collapse, ankylosis, or failed lesser procedures—not for a small osteophyte. Occlusal reconstruction is not a treatment for DJD. Systemic ketorolac is inappropriate given GERD and is not a chronic therapy.

title: High Axis II Burden — Why Irreversible Dental Treatment Fails
short: 29F • ASA II • GCPS Grade III • PHQ-9 = 16 • Multiple failed splints/equilibrations

patient.medical_history: Fibromyalgia, PTSD, major depressive disorder. Prior unsuccessful occlusal equilibration and two anterior bite planes that ‘made pain worse’.
patient.social_history: Disability paperwork pending. High catastrophizing (PCS elevated).
patient.chief_complaint: My bite is off and I need my teeth shaved or crowned so my jaw will finally go back in place. Nothing has helped.

clinical_findings.range_of_motion: Opening 42 mm, slow and guarded. Diffuse bilateral masseter/temporalis tenderness. Joints minimally tender. No locking. No crepitus.
clinical_findings.occlusion: Angle Class I. 1 mm CR-MIP slide, within normal. No pathologic wear. Prior enamel ‘equilibration’ facets on palatal #6–11.
clinical_findings.axis_II: GCPS Grade III (high pain intensity, high disability). PHQ-9 = 16 (moderately severe depression). GAD-7 = 14. Sleep poor. JFLR high.
clinical_findings.imaging: CBCT: normal condyles. MRI not indicated at this step.

flags: Axis I: likely local myalgia / myofascial pain — not a bite problem
Axis II: high disability, depression, catastrophizing — dominant prognostic factor
Prior irreversible occlusal treatment worsened symptoms
Biopsychosocial care, not more dentistry
guidelines: DC/TMD Axis II (GCPS, PHQ-9, GAD-7)
National Academies / AAOP: TMD is a biopsychosocial chronic pain disorder; irreversible occlusal therapy is not first-line

vignette.demographics: 29-year-old female with fibromyalgia, PTSD, depression on duloxetine/prazosin.
vignette.chief: Requests occlusal equilibration or crowns because ‘the bite is off’ after failed appliances.
vignette.clinical: Opening 42 mm, diffuse myofascial tenderness, joints quiet, 1 mm CR-MIP slide, prior enamel reduction.

questions.q: The strongest predictor of persistent pain and failed dental intervention in this patient is:
options: The 1 mm CR-MIP slide
High Axis II scores (GCPS III, depression, catastrophizing) reflecting a centralized/chronic overlapping pain phenotype
Failure to obtain a neuromuscular bite registration
Absence of a CBCT
questions.explanation: DC/TMD Axis II instruments exist because psychosocial burden and pain-related disability predict chronicity far better than millimeter occlusal slides. A 1 mm slide is within normal. ‘Neuromuscular’ registration and more imaging do not treat central sensitization, depression, or PTSD. This is a chronic overlapping pain condition (fibromyalgia + TMD).

questions.q: The most appropriate plan is:
options: Full-mouth reconstruction to a new vertical dimension this month

Decline further irreversible occlusal treatment; coordinate multidisciplinary care (orofacial pain, behavioral health/CBT, sleep, graded PT, medications already directed at centralized pain) and use only reversible dental measures
Repeat equilibration until the patient reports the bite feels ‘locked in’
Extract all remaining teeth and place All-on-4 because dentures cannot have TMD
questions.explanation: Irreversible occlusal therapy is contraindicated as a treatment for chronic TMD, especially after prior worsening. The evidence-based path is multidisciplinary chronic-pain care. Full-mouth reconstruction and elective full-arch extraction are harmful overtreatment. Edentulism does not cure TMD and often worsens it.

title: MAD-Related Occlusal Change and Joint Pain in a Patient with OSA
short: 52M • ASA II • MAD × 18 months • New posterior open bite • TMJ pain

patient.medical_history: Moderate OSA (AHI 22) using a custom titratable MAD because of CPAP intolerance. Controlled HTN.
patient.social_history: Never smoker. Compliant with MAD 6–7 nights/week.
patient.chief_complaint: My back teeth don’t touch anymore in the morning, and my jaw joints ache. The appliance still helps my sleep.

clinical_findings.occlusion: Bilateral posterior open bite of 1.5 mm at first molars in the morning, partially recovering by afternoon. Anterior coupling increased. Canine guidance flattened. Pre-MAD models (available) show previous posterior contacts.
clinical_findings.tmd_exam: Opening 40 mm. Bilateral TMJ arthralgia on lateral-pole palpation. Mild masseter tenderness. No lock.
clinical_findings.osa: Subjective residual snoring none. Partner reports no witnessed apneas. No follow-up sleep study since titration 14 months ago.
clinical_findings.imaging: CBCT not required first-line; condyles appear within a normal range on a screening panoramic.

flags: Known MAD adverse effect: occlusal changes (posterior open bite, mesial molar movement)
AADSM: informed consent and morning occlusal exercises / AM aligner
Do not ‘fix’ the bite with crowns while the MAD is still in use without a plan
Re-evaluate OSA efficacy with objective testing if titration is old
guidelines: AADSM clinical guidelines for oral appliance therapy — side effects and follow-up
DC/TMD arthralgia management; never jump to irreversible prosthodontics for appliance-induced bite change

vignette.demographics: 52-year-old male, moderate OSA on a custom MAD after CPAP failure. HTN.
vignette.chief: Morning posterior open bite and joint ache; MAD still helps sleep.
vignette.clinical: 1.5 mm posterior open bite mornings, partial recovery later; TMJ arthralgia; opening 40 mm.
vignette.endo: Teeth vital; this is not pulpal pain.

questions.q: The posterior open bite is best explained as:
options: An unrelated sudden condylar resorption syndrome in all MAD users
A recognized, often partly reversible dental/skeletal side effect of mandibular advancement (molar intrusion/mesialization and muscle/ligament adaptation)
Proof the appliance is counterfeit
Pathognomonic evidence of a need for four quadrants of crown lengthening
questions.explanation: AADSM literature documents occlusal changes in a substantial fraction of long-term MAD users: decreased overjet/overbite, mesial shift of mandibular molars, and posterior open bite. Morning exercises and a daytime occlusal jig reduce but do not always prevent them. This is not automatic condylar resorption and not an indication for crown lengthening.

questions.q: The most appropriate dental management now is:
options: Full-mouth crowns to ‘close the bite’ while continuing the MAD unchanged

Pause or retitrate the MAD, institute morning occlusal exercises/AM positioner, manage arthralgia conservatively, discuss CPAP retry or combination therapy, and delay any irreversible prosthodontics until a stable occlusion (and updated sleep study) exist
Immediate TMJ surgery
Tell the patient occlusal change means the appliance must be abandoned with no alternative
questions.explanation: Irreversible prosthodontics performed on a still-changing, appliance-driven occlusion will fail and may worsen TMD. Standard care is reversible: exercises, possible reduction of protrusion, temporary discontinuation if arthralgia is significant, conservative TMD care, and a new sleep study to confirm that MAD remains indicated versus CPAP/combination therapy. Surgery is not first-line. OSA still needs treatment—so abandonment without a plan is unsafe; involve sleep medicine.

Extractions in irradiated bone require atraumatic technique, antibiotics, possible HBO consultation per institutional protocol

guidelines: NCCN / AAOMS principles for dental care in irradiated patients

questions.q: What is the most appropriate management approach for extraction in this irradiated mandible?
options: Extract without any special precautions because radiation was >1 year ago
Atraumatic extraction, primary closure if possible, perioperative antibiotics, and consideration of institutional ORN-prevention protocols (including possible HBO consultation)
Always perform radical alveolectomy
Hyperbaric oxygen is proven to eliminate all ORN risk and is mandatory in every case
questions.explanation: ORN risk persists indefinitely after high-dose radiation. AAOMS and oncology guidelines emphasize atraumatic surgery, infection control, and individualized use of adjuncts such as HBO according to institutional protocols and patient factors.

guidelines: DoD Dental Readiness Classification system
Military dental deployment standards

questions.q: Under the DoD Dental Readiness Classification, this service member is currently:
options: DRC 1 — deployable, no treatment needed
DRC 2 — deployable with minor treatment that can be deferred
DRC 3 — non-deployable until the urgent/acute condition is resolved
DRC 4 — overdue for annual exam only
questions.explanation: Acute infection with swelling requiring urgent care classifies the member as DRC 3 (non-deployable). Treatment to a stable state (DRC 1 or 2) is required before deployment to an austere environment.

guidelines: DoD DRC definitions
Military dental readiness policies

DRC 2 — treatment indicated but member remains deployable if treatment is completed or the condition is judged low immediate risk
DRC 3 — non-deployable
DRC 4 — administrative
questions.explanation: DRC 2 covers oral conditions that require treatment but do not currently prevent deployment. Deep caries that could become symptomatic during a long austere deployment should be addressed pre-deployment whenever feasible.

title: Field Management — Avulsed Tooth During Training
short: 21M • Active Duty • Avulsed #8 • 25 min extra-oral dry time

patient.medical_history: Healthy.

clinical_findings.extraoral: Lip laceration, no concussion signs.
clinical_findings.intraoral: Socket #8 empty, socket walls intact, no alveolar fracture palpable. Adjacent teeth stable.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Field radiograph unavailable; clinical exam only.

flags: Avulsion with >15–20 min dry time significantly reduces PDL viability
IADT guidelines still guide replantation decision
Field constraints may limit endodontic follow-up
guidelines: IADT 2020 Dental Trauma Guidelines
Military field dental protocols

vignette.demographics: 21M active duty, field training, avulsed #8, 25 min dry time.
vignette.chief: Complete avulsion of maxillary central.
vignette.clinical: Intact socket, no alveolar fracture, dry storage.

questions.q: According to IADT guidelines, what is the preferred immediate management?
options: Do not replant because dry time exceeded 15 minutes

Replant after gentle rinsing, stabilize, and plan for endodontic therapy within 2 weeks (extra-oral dry time >15–20 min still warrants attempt at replantation in most cases, with informed prognosis discussion)
Immediate implant placement in the field
Only soft-tissue closure of the socket
questions.explanation: IADT recommends attempting replantation even after extended dry time, while counseling the patient about the high risk of replacement resorption and the need for timely endodontic treatment. Field conditions do not change the biologic rationale.

title: DRC & Third-Molar Decision Before Deployment
short: 23M • Active Duty • Asymptomatic mesioangular #32 • Long deployment

flags: Asymptomatic third molars with operculum and deep probing can become acute in austere environments
IAN proximity elevates surgical risk — shared decision
Pre-deployment extraction of high-risk thirds is often favored
guidelines: Military third-molar deployment policies
AAOMS white papers on third molars

vignette.demographics: 23M active duty, long austere deployment in 60 days.
vignette.chief: Asymptomatic partially erupted #32 under review for extraction.
vignette.clinical: Operculum, PD 5 mm distal, no acute infection.

questions.q: In the context of a long austere deployment, the most defensible recommendation is often:
options: Leave all asymptomatic third molars regardless of operculum or probing depth
Extract high-risk partially erupted third molars with opercula and deep distal probing before deployment, after informed consent regarding IAN risk
Only extract if the patient is already in pain
Coronectomy is never appropriate near the IAN
questions.explanation: Military dental readiness doctrine favors eliminating conditions likely to cause field emergencies. Partially erupted thirds with opercula are high-risk for pericoronitis during deployment; extraction (or coronectomy when IAN risk is extreme) after counseling is frequently recommended.

flags: Primary tooth intrusion — risk to permanent successor
IADT primary tooth trauma guidelines
Spontaneous re-eruption often preferred if permanent tooth not displaced
guidelines: IADT 2020 Guidelines for Primary Teeth

vignette.chief: Intruded maxillary primary incisor.

options: Immediate surgical repositioning and splinting in all cases
Allow spontaneous re-eruption and monitor clinically and radiographically; extract if the tooth fails to re-erupt or shows signs of infection or interference with the successor
Immediate extraction and space maintainer
Endodontic treatment through the intruded position
questions.explanation: IADT recommends observation for spontaneous re-eruption when the permanent tooth is not displaced. Extraction is reserved for cases with interference, infection, or failure to re-erupt.

options: Extraction and space maintenance in every case
Indirect pulp therapy or stepwise caries removal with well-sealed restoration when residual dentin remains and the tooth is asymptomatic
Pulpectomy as first-line for all deep caries
No treatment until abscess forms
questions.explanation: AAPD supports indirect pulp therapy for vital primary teeth with deep caries when there are no clinical or radiographic signs of irreversible pulpitis or necrosis, provided a hermetic seal can be achieved.

title: Space Management — Premature Loss of Primary Molar
short: 7M • ASA I • Extracted #I due to abscess • Space maintenance

Band-and-loop or other space maintainer indicated when successor is not imminent
AAPD / orthodontic space-management guidelines

options: No space maintenance is ever needed
Placement of an appropriate space maintainer (e.g., band-and-loop) and periodic monitoring
Immediate extraction of the contralateral primary molar for symmetry
Only fixed orthodontic appliances
questions.explanation: Space maintainers prevent mesial drift and space loss when the permanent successor will not erupt imminently. Band-and-loop is a classic choice for unilateral primary first-molar loss.

AAO / growth-modification principles
guidelines: Contemporary orthodontic growth-modification evidence

vignette.clinical: OJ 8 mm, lip incompetence, Class II molars.

questions.q: For a growing Class II division 1 patient at CS2–CS3 with large overjet, the most evidence-supported early intervention is often:
options: Wait until all permanent teeth erupt and then extract premolars only
Growth modification (functional appliance or headgear) during the pubertal growth spurt combined with later comprehensive orthodontics as needed
Immediate surgical mandibular advancement
Only interproximal reduction
questions.explanation: The pubertal growth spurt (CS3–CS4) is the optimal window for functional appliances or other growth-modification approaches in Class II patients. Early treatment can reduce OJ, improve soft-tissue profile, and decrease trauma risk.

flags: Palatal canine impaction common; early extraction of primary canine can improve eruption path in selected cases
CBCT for precise localization and root relationship
Surgical exposure + orthodontic traction if interceptive measures fail

Extraction of the retained primary canine and observation or limited orthodontic space maintenance, with surgical exposure planned if the permanent canine does not improve its path
No treatment until age 18
Only removable appliances without extraction of the primary tooth
questions.explanation: Extraction of the primary canine is a well-supported interceptive procedure that can allow spontaneous improvement in the eruption path of a palatally displaced permanent canine when space is adequate. Further traction is used if needed.

flags: Orthodontically induced inflammatory root resorption is common but usually mild

Monitoring and force reduction when resorption is detected

Only endodontic treatment of all incisors
questions.explanation: Detection of resorption warrants documentation, reduction of force magnitude or intermittent treatment, and closer radiographic follow-up. Most mild cases stabilize with these measures.

title: Clear Aligner Limitations — Severe Crowding & Skeletal Discrepancy

flags: Clear aligners have limitations for severe crowding and skeletal discrepancies
Informed consent must address realistic outcomes and possible need for fixed appliances or surgery
Periodontal biotype affects expansion limits

Explain the limitations of aligners for severe crowding and skeletal Class III, discuss realistic goals, and present alternative or combined treatment plans including possible surgery or fixed appliances
Refuse any treatment
Expand aggressively beyond the alveolar housing without discussion
questions.explanation: Informed consent requires honest discussion of the biomechanical limits of clear aligners. Severe skeletal discrepancies and large arch-length deficiencies often need fixed appliances, extractions, or orthognathic surgery for optimal results.
